title: Concrete Graphs: Sort, Count and Compare
seo_title: Kindergarten Concrete graphs Worksheets: Free Math with Pictures and Answers (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Concrete or pictorial graphs as a visual tool for collecting and representing data: collecting data, creating a concrete graph, and describing, comparing, and discussing the findings
meta_desc: Free Kindergarten math worksheets on concrete graphs for the BC curriculum: sort and count, sorting rules, cube rows and towers, compare groups and picture graphs. 100 picture questions with answers.
key_big: Line the groups up at one start line, then count and compare.
key_sub: 1 cube or 1 picture is 1. The longest row has the most.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Sort the things into groups with one rule, like colour or kind.
  • Make a concrete graph: put each group in a row or a tower. Start every row at the same line.
  • 1 cube or 1 picture is 1. Count each row.
  • The longest row or tallest tower has the most. The shortest has the fewest.

Examples

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do
Counting all the things, not one kindSort first. Count only one group.
Not starting at the same lineLine up every row at the start, then compare.
Giving one number for how many moreMatch the rows up and count the extra ones.

faq.a: A graph made with real objects, such as cubes, toys or shoes, put in rows or towers so children can count and compare them.
A graph where each picture stands for one thing, such as one vote. It is the next step after a concrete graph.
It shows the groups side by side, so you can see which has the most, which has the fewest, and how many more.

faq.q: How can I make a graph at home?
faq.a: Sort socks, toy cars or snacks into groups, line each group up from one edge, and count each row.
